lines.text: This little wooden bird is about two thousand two hundred years old. It fits in the palm of your hand. And some people say it is not a bird at all, but a model aeroplane, carved two thousand years before the Wright brothers.
A glider, built by ancient Egyptians. Or copied from something they saw in the sky. You have probably seen the claim.
So tonight we do something no museum would allow. We treat it like a new aircraft, and put it through a full flight-test programme.
Pre-flight inspection. Logbook. Airframe. Three flight tests: by hand, in a wind tunnel, and inside a computer. Then we ask what it was really built to do.
Every claim gets a score. At the end, a verdict. Cleared for flight, or grounded. Let's begin.
Test card, item one. Pre-flight. The object sits in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, under special register number six three four seven.
It is fourteen point two centimetres long, with a wingspan of eighteen point three. Carved from sycamore wood. Weight, thirty-nine grams, according to the man who made it famous.
Already, a warning light. Popular accounts give its weight as fourteen grams, or thirty-one. For an aircraft, weight is everything, and nobody agrees on it.

It was found in eighteen ninety-eight, at Saqqara, the vast burial ground of ancient Memphis, in a tomb usually named as the tomb of Pa-di-Imen. It is dated to around two hundred B C, the age of the Ptolemies.
But the paperwork is thin. No excavation report has been published that shows exactly which tomb, or what lay beside it. Even the year wobbles. One scientific abstract says eighteen ninety-one.
So we have a real ancient object, a fuzzy birth certificate, and one strange shape. Now, the logbook. How did a bird become a plane?
Item two. The logbook. Nineteen sixty-nine. An Egyptian doctor, Khalil Messiha, is looking at a case of ancient bird models in the Cairo museum.
Messiha taught anatomy for artists, and he had built model aeroplanes since childhood. He belonged to model flying clubs. So when he looked at this one bird, he saw something the others did not show.
No legs. No painted feathers. Straight wings. And a tail that stands upright, like the fin of a plane. Real birds, he argued, hold their tails flat.
His brother Guirguis, a flight engineer, built a copy in balsa wood. Messiha added a horizontal tailplane, which he supposed had been lost, and wrote that it sailed a few yards when thrown by hand.
His conclusion was bold. This was a scale model of a full-size monoplane, and somewhere in Saqqara, the real aircraft might still be waiting.
In nineteen seventy-two the idea went public, in an Egyptian travel magazine. Reports say the Cairo museum even staged a small exhibition of ancient model aircraft, with the bird as its star.
Then the story started to grow. A journalist added a groove under the tail, where a tailplane would slot in. Messiha himself had described no groove, and no holes.

A magazine wrote that a separate slotted piece fits onto the tail, that it soars with a slight jerk of the hand, and that a full-size version could carry heavy loads. A newspaper gave it landing gear.
Online, it now carries hieroglyphs saying the gift of Amun, and three papyri nearby that say, I want to fly. None of that is in any record. Gift of Amun is simply what the tomb owner's name means.

One site even says Erich von Däniken used the bird in his nineteen sixty-eight bestseller. That book came out a year before anyone called it a plane. In the ancient astronaut world, it sits beside the golden jets of Colombia.
So the logbook shows one honest observation, and a pile of later upgrades. Time to inspect the airframe itself.
Item three. Airframe inspection. Let's look at it the way an aircraft engineer would, and the way an Egyptologist would.

First, the head. It has a beak and a painted eye. There is paint on the top of the tail, and two faint reddish lines around the belly. Underneath, the body curves from head to tail like a bird in flight.
Second, the wings. From the front, the tips droop downwards. Engineers call that anhedral. On a small glider, it makes things worse: it tips the model into a spiral.
Third, the wing joint. The wing is held on with iron nails, sits off-centre and slightly skewed. A glider expert concluded it had probably been remounted in modern times.

That expert is Martin Gregorie, who has designed and flown free-flight competition gliders for more than thirty years, and placed fifth at a world championship. He lists three things any stable glider needs.
One. The balance point must sit roughly a quarter to sixty percent back along the wing. The Saqqara bird balances at, or behind, the trailing edge. And no weight was ever put in its head.
Two. A horizontal tailplane, about a fifth to a quarter of the wing area. The bird has none, and there is no trace of where one was ever fixed.
Three. Wing tips raised, not lowered, to stop it rolling over. The bird has the opposite. Zero out of three.
On paper, the airframe fails inspection. But paper is not flight. So we do what the believers asked for. We fly it.

Flight test one. Hand launch. In two thousand two, Gregorie built balsa replicas from careful drawings, with two wings, and two tails: one to scale, and one large tailplane, a quarter of the wing area.
With no tail, or the scale tail, it would not fly. Launched slowly, it pitched up. Launched fast, it pitched down. Then it tumbled. Weight in the nose changed nothing.
But mounted on a pin under the wing, it did one job beautifully. It turned straight into the wind and held steady. Remember that.
With the big tailplane fitted, it finally glided, fast and steep. It could not be launched with a slight jerk of the hand. It needed a full-arm throw.
Best result: three metres forward for a one point three metre drop. A glide of one to two point three. A modern sailplane does better than one to forty.
Weighted up to match the real wood, he said it flew more like a brick with fins than an aircraft. His verdict: it never flew. More likely a toy, or a weather vane.
But believers had an answer. Hand launches are crude. Put it in a wind tunnel, and the numbers tell a different story.
Flight test two. The wind tunnel. In two thousand six, a television documentary had an aerodynamics specialist, Simon Sanderson, build a larger replica and put it in the airflow, with no tailplane.
The headline result: it produced four times its own weight in lift. Clips of that moment still circulate as proof.
But read the small print. The model was held in place by cables, and the cables did the stabilising. Lift is not flight. A flat plank makes lift. Keeping it pointed the right way is the hard part.

Then the programme took the data to a flight simulator at Liverpool University, and added a stabilising tailplane. With the tailplane, the simulated bird flew quite well. The part that made it fly was the part that was never found.

In two thousand eleven, for William Shatner's TV series Weird or What, Gregorie went further. New replicas, a mechanical launcher for repeatable throws, careful measurements, and the tailplane fitted.
The glide ratios came in between about two point two and two point eight. Gregorie put it plainly: that is about as good as a man in a wingsuit. Even the space shuttle glides better.
With the drooping scale wing, it rolled forty degrees within two metres. And without the tailplane, it tumbled, every time. Two tests, one pattern.
Flight test three. The digital twin. Replicas can be built wrong. So in twenty twenty-three, two engineers from the Institute of Aerospace Technology in Bremen tested the real shape.
Michel Zierow and Leon Lesemann used a 3D photo scan of the artefact, made with staff of the Egyptian Museum, rebuilt it in seventy-four slices, and ran a full computer airflow simulation.
Lift peaked at a low angle and then the flow broke away. Drag was two to five times that of a light aircraft. Best lift to drag ratio: two point eight six.

To glide at all, it would need about seventeen metres per second, roughly sixty kilometres an hour. Too fast, the authors wrote, for a stable launch by hand. Dropped from two metres, its best flight is five and a half metres, lasting one and a half seconds.
Its centre of gravity sits fifty-four millimetres behind the nose, near the trailing edge, behind the point that would keep it stable. So it pitches up.
And the lift is lopsided, stronger on the left wing. So it rolls right, banks, pitches up, stalls, and crashes. In their words, it cannot fly a straight path.
Three tests, three methods, one result. As it is, the Saqqara bird does not fly. But the engineers ended with a hint. Look at it as a cultural object. And that vertical fin might suit a weather vane.

Item seven. Alternate role. If not an aircraft, then what? Start with the temple walls. At Karnak, in the Temple of Khonsu, reliefs of sacred festival boats show small bird figures on top of their masts.
A bird on a pivot, with an upright fin, turns its beak into the wind. That is exactly what Gregorie's replica did. A wind vane, on a boat, a shrine or a roof, explains the strangest feature, the fin.
Or a sacred bird. The falcon was the form of Horus and of the sun god Ra-Horakhty. Egyptian bird figures were made for coffins, shrines and offerings, most with folded wings and painted feathers.

Or a toy. Wikipedia describes it as mounted on a stick. A child running with a wooden bird held high would make the same shape against the sky. Toy, vane, falcon, masthead: none of these is proven, but all of them fit.
And the era matters. Two hundred B C is the Ptolemaic age, a time of real invention: gears, screws, valves, Archimedes. Clever people lived then. But they left texts and machines behind.
For aviation, there is nothing. No full-size glider. No workshop. No text on flight. No image of a flying machine. Just one small wooden bird.
And the alien version, that it copies a craft visitors flew? It has even less: no craft, no visitors, and a model that cannot fly. It depends on reading a falcon's fin as a rudder.
Debrief. Time to score the Saqqara bird.

A real ancient carving, about two hundred B C: evidence. Shaped like a bird, with beak, eye and paint: evidence. An upright fin unlike other bird figures: real, and still open. A vane, a masthead, a toy or a falcon: likely.
A missing tailplane, or a groove for one: no trace. Flies as it is: debunked, by three separate tests. Alien or lost aviation knowledge: no evidence.

The verdict. Grounded. The Saqqara bird is a real and lovely carving of a bird, probably a vane, a sacred figure or a toy. It is not a glider, and it never was. But its fin is still a small, honest mystery.
Somewhere, twenty-two centuries ago, a carver made a bird with a tail that stands up. Maybe because it turned in the wind. That idea is wonderful enough, without aliens.
Next case: one man, more than a thousand tons of coral rock, and no witnesses. How did he move it?
What do you think the fin was for? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next ancient mystery put to the test.
